vm_tools: concierge: Run crosvm commands synchronously Currently concierge spawns a process to run a crosvm command but doesn't wait for it to exit. This is a problem at suspend time because concierge will report suspend readiness to powerd and the crosvm command process will race with the system going to suspend. If the system suspends before all vcpus have been stopped the guest kernel will panic on resume because it thinks there is a soft lockup. Always wait for the crosvm command process to complete before continuing. chromeos-chrome: Use compressed binary profiles Clang has grown support for a special type of AFDO profile called a 'compressed binary' profile. This profile format should be functionally identical to our current binary profiles, but allows for lazy loading of function profiles. Given that the incredible majority of TUs should only contain a very small subset of functions represented in the AFDO file, this is expected to save a large amount of RAM and CPU per TU. In practice, given 100 arbitrarily selected C++ compilations with AFDO enabled in Chrome -- I literally just grepped a build log of `ninja -v` and cleaned it up a bit -- we see: Old profile; Max wall-time: 3.29s Average wall-time: 1.055s Min wall-time: 0.84s Max RSS: 578,572KB Average RSS: 486,437KB Min RSS: 463,236KB New profile: Max wall-time: 2.51s Average wall time: 0.260s Min wall-time: 0.05s Max RSS: 158,236KB Average RSS: 64,629KB Min RSS: 40,828KB This is a reduction of ~800ms of CPU and 421.8MB of RAM per TU on average. This reduction should be roughly constant per TU (wall-time reduction for the max wall-times was ~780ms, and memory reduction for the maximum RSSes was 420,296KB), with larger TUs seeing slightly less reduction. Percentage savings are not presented here, since the majority of these randomly-selected compilations were small and quick. I suspect that trying to generalize savings percentages would be over-optimistic. Chrome has many 'heavier' compilations that take hundreds of MB of RAM and seconds of CPU without AFDO, and my fear is that this random set of compilations didn't have a representatively large sample of those. The point was just to show that the savings from lazy loading profiles is roughly constant, and it does appear to be. BUG=None TEST=Built Chrome with both 'regular' and 'compressed binary' profiles. They were bitwise identical.
